summary: HappyBee is a web map that helps migratory beekeepers and growers of insect-pollinated crops meet at the right place in the right week. For every week of the season it shows when each parcel blooms. Apple, sour cherry and black locust bloom is estimated from published heat-sum models run on NASA POWER temperatures. For sunflower the map shows the grower's declared window, with the NASA HLS yellowness index as satellite evidence. NASA SMAP root-zone soil moisture flags sunflower bloom on exceptionally dry soil, when nectar is at risk. Hive sites inside protected areas are blocked. Each match between a beekeeper and a parcel comes with its reasons and what is still missing, and a move calculator also says when not to move. Every value is labelled Observed, Estimated, Reported or Missing and carries a date, so an estimate cannot pass for a measurement. Furthermore, to ensure robust mapping of crops and protected habitats (such as Natura 2000), we have published a comprehensive visual and methodological validation on multi-sensor satellite data fusion. Through a direct manual comparison of optical Sentinel-2 imagery and Sentinel-1 SAR backscatter, we demonstrate how active microwave radar overcomes optical vulnerabilities (like cloud shadows), proving the necessity of SAR/NISAR integration for reliable, all-weather land-cover monitoring. Full methodology here: https://github.com/gabboraron/NASA_SpaceAppsChallenge2026-Terra_and_Luna_Analytics/wiki/Manual-Evaluation-&-Ground-Truth

Introduction

A grower needs suitable pollinating colonies during a short flowering window. A migratory beekeeper needs accessible forage and a placement whose expected return justifies moving and maintaining the hives. The same field can create value for both, but not necessarily at the same price or in the same direction of payment.

HappyBee brings flowering estimates, grower reports, satellite evidence, regional soil conditions and placement economics into one weekly map. The practical question is: where should these hives be placed this week, and is moving better than staying?

More about the problem: problem.md · gabboraron/NASA_SpaceAppsChallenge2026-Terra_and_Luna_Analytics Wiki · GitHub

HappyBee shows a season as 26 weeks on a map. For each parcel and week, it gives the bloom state, a dry-soil nectar flag, and the protected sites nearby. A beekeeper picks their apiary and gets a ranked list of parcels, each with the reasons for the match, the warnings, and what is still missing. A move calculator then compares the contribution after incremental costs with staying put, so the answer can be "do not move". The live demo needs no login: https://happybee.happyhill-b1bb4730.northeurope.azurecontainerapps.io ; also, the code is available: GitHub - gabboraron/NASA_SpaceAppsChallenge2026-Terra_and_Luna_Analytics: This is the repo of the Terra and Luna Analytics for the NASA Space Apps 2026 https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/find-a-team/terra-and-luna-analytics · GitHub

We estimate bloom for apple, sour cherry, and black locust from published heat-sum (growing degree day) models on NASA POWER daily temperatures, and show it next to the grower's declared window. For sunflower, we show the declared window with the NASA HLS yellowness index (NDYI) per parcel and week as satellite evidence. NASA SMAP L4 root-zone soil moisture is compared with its 2015 to 2024 record for the same place, and sunflower bloom on exceptionally dry soil is flagged as nectar at risk. That rule is a labelled heuristic. It works at the scale of a roughly 9 km cell, so it describes the area around a parcel. Hive sites inside protected areas are blocked, and sites close to one raise a warning.

Beekeepers avoid costly moves to a bloom that is late, over, or dry, and growers get hives when their crop actually flowers. Protected habitats stay out of the matching. The demo has two seasons, a drought year (2022) and a normal year (2024), and the same week looks very different in each.

What we think is new is the labelling. Every number is marked Observed, Estimated, Reported, or Missing, with its source and date. Interpolated weeks are marked as interpolated, and when a NASA source fails, the value is shown as Missing with the reason.

NASA data is global, so the method is not tied to one country, although the demo runs on one pilot region. The beekeepers and growers in the demo are synthetic, and the parcels are illustrative. Both are labelled in the app, and it holds no personal data. Each model parameter cites a published source. A separate verification folder compares the bloom models with hive-scale weight records and dated field observations from past years, and lists what the models cannot yet show. We make no yield claims.

Technical introduction

The logic behind our technical pipeline is straightforward: by combining phenological blooming calendars with an optical vegetation classifier (Sentinel-2/HLS), we can pinpoint exactly where and when target allergenic plants are active. To quantify their actual volume, we estimate structural biomass using NISAR radar data (via the Radar Vegetation Index). However, since radar backscatter is sensitive to water content, we fuse it with antecedent soil moisture and humidity data (NASA SMAP & POWER) to filter out weather-induced artifacts and false positives.

The server is written in Python 3.12 with FastAPI, pydantic, httpx, shapely, pyproj, earthaccess, rasterio and h5py. The map client uses React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre, and Terra Draw. Docker, GitHub Actions and Azure Container Apps build and host it. We used Claude Code and GitHub Copilot for research and code. The team came up with the idea and reviewed every change (see AI_USAGE.md in the repository).

More about the workflow at: workflow.md · gabboraron/NASA_SpaceAppsChallenge2026-Terra_and_Luna_Analytics Wiki · GitHub

Validation of the model

The product predicts when a crop blooms and whether nectar is likely. We do not use pollen forecast APIs: they cover wind-pollinated allergen taxa, cannot rewind past seasons, and are themselves model outputs. Instead we compare the running API's timeline for past demo years with independent measurements:

Validation is a left-to-right pipeline: gather inputs, derive comparable signals on both sides, run one scenario per question, then judge and write the report. Years under test default to 2022 and 2024. Timeline weeks start on 1 March; Hive and iNaturalist dates stay on the calendar, so every comparison is by date.

Business plan

HappyBee is a proposed marketplace connecting growers seeking pollination services with beekeepers offering hives. Growers can publish their crop, location, and expected flowering window; beekeepers can find opportunities and assess whether a move makes financial sense. The proposed revenue model is a commission on completed pollination bookings, with optional paid planning tools for professional users. We would start in Hungary through partnerships with local beekeepers and grower associations, validate the service over a flowering season, and expand as participation grows. The current demo demonstrates matching and decision support; commercial bookings are a planned next step.
